## Introduction

Electronic Health Record (EHR) data are longitudinal but not collected by design. Patients visit at irregular times, and even when a visit occurs, an outcome or biomarker may not be measured. **CIMEHR** provides simple benchmark methods and semiparametric joint models for analyses affected by informative visiting and informative observation.

This vignette starts with the data format, then moves from simpler baseline methods to the more complex CIMEHR estimators.

```{r load-package}
library(CIMEHR)
```

## 1. Input data format

The analysis functions expect **long-format data**, with one row per subject-visit or subject-time record. For the primary CIMEHR estimators, the default columns are:

| Column role | Default name | Meaning |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Subject identifier | `id` | Unique subject ID |
| Visit time | `time` | Visit time; rows with `NA` in `time` are treated as unvisited rows |
| Outcome | `Y` | Longitudinal outcome; typically `NA` when unobserved |
| Observation indicator | `R` | 1 if `Y` is observed at a visit, 0 otherwise |
| Censoring/follow-up end | `C` | End of follow-up for each subject |
| Covariates | e.g., `Z`, `X` | Baseline or model covariates |

All package methods should be given long/panel data. Some simpler benchmark methods analyze only observed outcome rows internally, but the user-supplied dataset should still contain aligned visit times, observation indicators, outcomes, and covariates in long format.

### 1.1 Converting short/wide data to long data

If your dataset has one row per subject and repeated visit/outcome columns, reshape it first:

```{r wide-to-long, eval = FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

wide_dat <- tibble::tibble(
  id = 1:2,
  Z = c(0, 1),
  X = c(0.2, -0.4),
  C = c(60, 60),
  time_1 = c(5, 8),  time_2 = c(20, NA), time_3 = c(45, 50),
  Y_1 = c(1.2, NA), Y_2 = c(1.6, NA), Y_3 = c(2.0, 1.1)
)

long_dat <- wide_dat %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = matches("^(time|Y)_\\\\d+$"),
    names_to = c(".value", "visit"),
    names_pattern = "(time|Y)_(\\\\d+)"
  ) %>%
  mutate(R = as.integer(!is.na(Y))) %>%
  arrange(id, time)
```

For CIMEHR-family methods, you can also use custom column names:

```{r custom-column-names, eval = FALSE}
fit <- CIMEHR(
  data = my_data,
  id_col = "patient_id",
  time_col = "visit_time",
  y_col = "hba1c",
  r_col = "measured",
  censor_col = "followup_end",
  covars_visit_XV = c("age", "female"),
  covars_outcome_fixed_XY = c("age", "female"),
  covars_outcome_random_link_ZY = "female",
  covars_obs_fixed_XO = c("age", "female"),
  covars_obs_random_link_ZO = "female"
)
```

## 2. Example dataset

The package includes `sim_ehr_data`, generated from a model with informative visiting, informative observation, and a longitudinal outcome process.

```{r load-data}
data("sim_ehr_data")
head(sim_ehr_data)
```

The true simulation parameters are stored as an attribute:

```{r true-params}
true_params <- attr(sim_ehr_data, "true_params")
true_params$beta
true_params$gamma
```

## 3. Method comparison

### Outcome-only

| Method | IP | IO | Shared Latent | Adjustment Mechanism | Package |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--|:--|:--|
| Summary statistics | ✗ | ✗ | None | Reduces the longitudinal series to a single scalar (e.g., min, mean, median, max) for regression. | — |
| Standard LMM (Laird and Ware, 1982) | ✗ | ✗ | None | Conditions on observed covariates (valid only under MAR). | lme4 |
| VA-LMM (Goldstein et al., 2016) | ✓ | ✗ | None | Includes *visit count* as a fixed covariate proxy. | lme4 |
| OA-LMM | ✗ | ✓ | None | Includes *observation count* as a fixed covariate proxy. | lme4 |

### IP-only

| Method | IP | IO | Shared Latent | Adjustment Mechanism | Package |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--|:--|:--|
| Liang (Liang et al., 2009) | ✓ | ✗ | Visiting & Outcome | Joint likelihood estimation via shared frailty linking visiting and outcome. | IrregLong |
| JMVL-G (Gasparini et al., 2020) | ✓ | ✗ | Visiting & Outcome | Joint likelihood modeling inter-visit times via shared random effects. | merlin |
| IIRR-Weighting (Burzykova and Lumley, 2007) | ✓ | ✗ | None | Inverse intensity weighting based on visiting intensity. | — |
| IIRR-Balanced (Yiu and Su, 2025) | ✓ | ✗ | None | Inverse intensity weighting adjusted for covariate balance. | — |
| Pairwise Likelihood (PairLik) (Chen et al., 2015) | ✓ | ✗ | None | Constructs a likelihood from all within-subject pairs of observations; conditioning on observed visit times eliminates the visit intensity from the likelihood. | — |

### Imputation + IP-only

| Method | IP | IO | Shared Latent | Adjustment Mechanism | Package |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--|:--|:--|
| Multiple Imputation (MI) (Rubin, 1987) | ✓ | ✓ | Determined by IP-only | Multiple imputation based on posterior draws, followed by IP-only methods. | mice |
| Linear Increment Methods (LI) (Aalen and Gunnes, 2010) | ✓ | ✓ | Determined by IP-only | Deterministic linear interpolation between observed visits to impute missing values, followed by IP-only methods. | slim |

### IP+IO

| Method | IP | IO | Shared Latent | Adjustment Mechanism | Package |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--|:--|:--|
| Adapted-Liang (Liang et al., 2009) | ✓ | ✓ | Visiting & Outcome | Joint model structure defined, but observation coefficients are constrained to zero. | — |
| EHRJoint (Du et al., 2025) | ✓ | ✓ | Visiting & Outcome | Tripartite model; observation process modeled via covariates only (no latent link). | — |
| Proposed (this package) | ✓ | ✓ | All three processes | Tripartite model; full shared latent structure links Visiting, Observation, and Outcome. | CIMEHR |

IP = informative visiting / informative presence adjustment; IO = informative observation adjustment.
The “Proposed” row corresponds to `CIMEHR()`; `CIMEHR_timevarying_ghq()` and `CIMEHR_timevarying_ou()` extend this framework with more flexible observation-process modeling.

## 4. Simpler benchmark methods first

### 4.1 Summary-statistic regression

`Summary_stat()` is a naive baseline that collapses each subject's observed outcomes to a summary statistic and fits a cross-sectional regression.

```{r summarystat, eval = FALSE}
fit_ss <- Summary_stat(
  sim_ehr_data,
  formula = ~ Z + X
)
print(fit_ss)
summary(fit_ss)
```

### 4.2 Linear mixed model

`Linear_mixed_model()` wraps `nlme::lme()` and supports standard, observation-adjusted, and visit-adjusted variants.

```{r lmm, eval = FALSE}
fit_lmm <- Linear_mixed_model(
  sim_ehr_data,
  fixed = Y ~ Z + X + time,
  random = ~ 1 + Z | id,
  obs_indicator = "R"
)
print(fit_lmm)
summary(fit_lmm)

fit_va <- Linear_mixed_model(
  sim_ehr_data,
  fixed = Y ~ Z + X + time,
  random = ~ 1 + Z | id,
  obs_indicator = "R",
  visit_adjust = "VA"
)
```

### 4.3 Pairwise likelihood

`Pairwise_likelihood()` fits a pairwise composite likelihood model for observed outcomes.

```{r pairwise, eval = FALSE}
obs_data <- sim_ehr_data[sim_ehr_data$R == 1 & !is.na(sim_ehr_data$R), ]

fit_pl <- Pairwise_likelihood(
  data = obs_data,
  formula = Y ~ Z + X + time,
  pair_sample = 5000
)
summary(fit_pl)
```

## 5. Visiting-process adjustment methods

### 5.1 Inverse intensity rate ratio weighting

```{r iirr, eval = FALSE}
fit_iirr <- Inverse_intensity_rate_ratio_weighting(
  sim_ehr_data,
  visit_covs = c("Z", "X")
)
summary(fit_iirr)
```

### 5.2 Inverse intensity rate ratio balancing

```{r iirr-bal, eval = FALSE}
fit_bal <- Inverse_intensity_rate_ratio_balancing(
  sim_ehr_data,
  visit_covs = c("Z", "X")
)
summary(fit_bal)
```

### 5.3 Liang--Lu--Ying joint visiting/outcome model

```{r liang, eval = FALSE}
fit_liang <- Joint_modeling_visiting_and_longitudinal_Liang(
  sim_ehr_data,
  visit_covs = c("Z", "X"),
  long_covs = c("Z", "X"),
  random_covs = "Z"
)
summary(fit_liang)
```

### 5.4 EHRJoint

`EHRJoint()` is a joint benchmark method. Its summary output notes that its observation process uses a logistic regression with a logit link.

```{r ehrjoint, eval = FALSE}
fit_ej <- EHRJoint(
  sim_ehr_data,
  visit_covs = c("Z", "X"),
  long_covs = c("Z", "X"),
  random_covs = "Z"
)
summary(fit_ej)
```

## 6. Primary CIMEHR methods

### 6.1 Base CIMEHR

`CIMEHR()` jointly models informative visiting, informative observation, and the longitudinal outcome. Its visiting process uses Andersen--Gill partial likelihood with log-normal frailty, and its observation process uses a probit model with latent-random-link random effects when specified.

```{r cimehr, eval = FALSE}
fit_cimehr <- CIMEHR(
  data = sim_ehr_data,
  covars_visit_XV = c("Z", "X"),
  covars_outcome_fixed_XY = c("Z", "X"),
  covars_outcome_random_link_ZY = "Z",
  covars_obs_fixed_XO = c("Z", "X"),
  covars_obs_random_link_ZO = "Z"
)

print(fit_cimehr)
summary(fit_cimehr)
coef(fit_cimehr)
confint(fit_cimehr)
```

### 6.2 CIMEHR with Gauss--Hermite quadrature

`CIMEHR_timevarying_ghq()` uses Gauss--Hermite quadrature and online filtering for a more flexible observation process. Analytic standard errors are not currently exposed, so bootstrap inference is recommended.

```{r cimehr-ghq, eval = FALSE}
fit_ghq <- CIMEHR_timevarying_ghq(
  data = sim_ehr_data,
  gh_points_U = 7,
  gh_points_q = 5
)
summary(fit_ghq)
```

### 6.3 CIMEHR with OU pairwise composite likelihood

`CIMEHR_timevarying_ou()` models serial correlation in the observation process using an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck process and pairwise composite likelihood.

```{r cimehr-ou, eval = FALSE}
fit_ou <- CIMEHR_timevarying_ou(
  data = sim_ehr_data,
  pair_type = "adjacent"
)
summary(fit_ou)
confint(fit_ou)
```

## 7. Bootstrap inference

Several methods do not provide closed-form standard errors. `bootstrap()` resamples subjects with replacement and refits the selected method.

```{r bootstrap, eval = FALSE}
bs <- bootstrap(
  fit_iirr,
  data = sim_ehr_data,
  B = 200,
  seed = 1
)
print(bs)
summary(bs)
```

For CIMEHR-family methods, use the new symmetric argument names when forwarding covariate specifications:

```{r bootstrap-cimehr, eval = FALSE}
bs_cimehr <- bootstrap(
  fit_cimehr,
  data = sim_ehr_data,
  B = 200,
  seed = 1,
  covars = list(
    covars_visit_XV = c("Z", "X"),
    covars_outcome_fixed_XY = c("Z", "X"),
    covars_outcome_random_link_ZY = "Z",
    covars_obs_fixed_XO = c("Z", "X"),
    covars_obs_random_link_ZO = "Z"
  )
)
```

## 8. Simulating custom data

```{r custom-sim, eval = FALSE}
dat <- sim_data_gen(
  n = 2000,
  seed = 42,
  gamma = c(intercept = -2.0, Z = 0.8, X = 0.5),
  beta = c(intercept = -1.0, Z = -1.0, X = 0.3),
  sigma_zeta = 0.8,
  phi = 0.2
)

fit <- CIMEHR(data = dat$long_data)
summary(fit)
```

Du, J., Shi, X., and Mukherjee, B. (2025). A new statistical approach for joint modeling of longitudinal outcomes measured in electronic health records with clinically informative presence and observation processes.

Goldstein, B. A., Bhavsar, N. A., Phelan, M., and Pencina, M. J. (2016). Controlling for informed presence bias due to the number of health encounters in an electronic health record. *American Journal of Epidemiology*, 184, 847--855.

Rubin, D. (1987). *Multiple imputation for nonresponse in surveys*. John Wiley & Sons, New York.

Yiu, S. and Su, L. (2025). Accommodating informative visit times for analysing irregular longitudinal data: A sensitivity analysis approach with balancing weights estimators. *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series C: Applied Statistics*, 74, 824--843.
